Andrew Cant
an'drū' kant
n. (Andrew Cant, c. 1590–1663, Covenanting preacher of Aberdeen, a Protester)
Greek Andreas, manly; Cant, a Scottish surname. The English word cant, whining jargon, was wrongly derived from his name by eighteenth-century writers; it is in fact from Latin cantare, to sing.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Andrew Cant was the most formidable Covenanting preacher in the north-east of Scotland. Minister successively at Alford, Newbattle and from 1641 at Aberdeen, he was sent in 1638 with Alexander Henderson and David Dickson to carry the National Covenant to Aberdeen, the most royalist and Episcopal city in the kingdom, and preached it there against the Aberdeen Doctors and a hostile magistracy. He sat in the Westminster Assembly's Scottish delegation's orbit, served as a chaplain in the Covenanting armies, and took the Protesters' side in 1651. His plainness made enemies and made a legend: Samuel Johnson's dictionary and others after him derived the English word cant, for whining sanctimonious talk, from his preaching, which is an etymological slander — the word comes from the Latin for singing — but which shows how a certain kind of preaching was remembered. He was deprived in 1660 and died in 1663. “But truly I am full of power by the spirit of the LORD” (Mic 3:8).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines cant as a whining, affected or hypocritical manner of speaking, and boldness as freedom from timidity in speaking.

expand to see more

CANT, n. A whining, affected or hypocritical manner of speech; the particular jargon of a class or profession.

BOLD'NESS, n. Courage; freedom from timidity in speaking or writing; assurance.

COV'ENANTER, n. One who makes a covenant; in Scotland, an adherent of the National Covenant.

PLAIN'NESS, n. Openness; rough sincerity; freedom from ornament or ambiguity.

Key Scripture

Mic 3:8 — "But truly I am full of power by the spirit of the LORD, and of judgment, and of might, to declare unto Jacob his transgression, and to Israel his sin."

Act 4:13 — "Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marvelled; and they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus."

Jer 20:9 — "Then I said, I will not make mention of him, nor speak any more in his name. But his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay."

1Co 2:4 — "And my speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of man's wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power:"

Modern Corruption

The Aberdeen Covenanter whose name was wrongly made an English word for hypocrisy.

expand to see more

The false etymology that turned Cant's surname into a word for sanctimonious whining did real work, and the work it did is still being done. It is the oldest and most effective answer to plain preaching: not to refute it but to assign it a tone, so that any man who speaks directly about sin can be dismissed as canting. The device requires no argument and is therefore always available.

The principle to recover is that the prophet's plainness is a gift of the Spirit and not a temperament, and that its content is specified: “to declare unto Jacob his transgression, and to Israel his sin” (Mic 3:8). Jeremiah records what it costs to keep silent instead: “But his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay” (Jer 20:9).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew koach (H3581), power; Greek parrhesia (G3954), boldness of speech.

Usage

"“to declare unto Jacob his transgression, and to Israel his sin” (Mic 3:8) — Aberdeen, 1638."

"“they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus” (Act 4:13) — the plainness that was mistaken for cant."

"“not with enticing words of man's wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power” (1Co 2:4) — his register."
